strengths: TPCs offer a simple, coherent construction: progressively trained polynomial terms preserve the original linear probe and support both fixed-budget truncation and confidence-based early exits.
The empirical coverage is substantial: four LLMs, two datasets, multiple layers, five seeds for the main comparisons, and extensive rank, degree, factorization, and training ablations.
Comparisons include individually tuned, parameter-matched MLPs and early-exit MLPs. Results show consistent improvements over linear probes and competitive nonlinear-probe performance.
The polynomial representation permits exact algebraic attribution of individual interaction terms, and the appendix provides useful implementation and optimization details.
weaknesses: The BeaverTails task definition is insufficiently justified. Its standard safety annotations concern responses in prompt–response pairs, whereas the paper describes them as harmful-prompt labels and uses prompt representations. The manuscript must clarify the actual input, label construction, and handling of repeated prompts across splits. Otherwise, a major portion of the evaluation may measure a different task from the one claimed.

The central efficiency claim is only partially demonstrated. Cascade experiments measure cumulative parameter usage, while Appendix G.2 benchmarks fixed exits rather than actual adaptive execution. Routing, shrinking batches, synchronization, and activation extraction are not measured. Figure 3 supports savings relative to the full polynomial, but does not establish the repeated claim of costs only slightly above a linear probe; each additional rank-64 term costs roughly 64 linear-probe evaluations.

The safety conclusions exceed the evaluation. Aggregate F1 and calibration plots do not establish harmful-request recall at controlled false-positive rates or the reliability of confident early exits. Despite adversarial examples in WildGuardMix, there is no adaptive attack evaluation or explicit cross-dataset transfer study. Several curves are nonmonotonic, so additional terms do not reliably purchase stronger guardrails.

The novelty is primarily a combination of established polynomial networks, stagewise additive training, and confidence-based cascades. Missing comparisons to a simple linear-probe-to-MLP cascade and progressively trained additive MLPs leave unclear whether polynomial interactions are necessary. The progressive-training ablation compares against training only the final output, rather than a joint objective supervising every truncation.

The bilinear baseline is problematic as specified: zᵀAᵀAz is nonnegative, so applying a sigmoid and the usual 0.5 threshold cannot produce harmless predictions without an additional bias or threshold adjustment. Neither is documented for this baseline. Training comparisons also give progressive TPCs 50 epochs per term versus 50 epochs total for joint models, requiring a training-budget sensitivity check.

Interpretability evidence is limited to an algebraic decomposition of one quadratic example. The displayed interactions contribute approximately 0.005 each to a total logit of 18.11, without demonstrating explanatory coverage, semantic meaning, or useful analysis of the deployed degree-five classifier. Exact decomposition supports attribution, but not the broader claim of practically interpretable safety decisions.

strengths: The method is clear and useful: progressively trained polynomial terms yield nested classifiers that recover a linear probe exactly and support both fixed-budget and confidence-based evaluation.
The experimental coverage is substantial, including four LLMs, two datasets, parameter-matched MLP and early-exit MLP baselines, hyperparameter searches, and five-seed fixed-order comparisons.

The appendix contains meaningful ablations of progressive training, polynomial degree, rank, and symmetric factorization, alongside calibration and latency measurements. Results demonstrate competitive classification performance and promising cascade tradeoffs.
Polynomial coefficients provide exact algebraic attribution of neuron interactions to classifier logits, although their semantic interpretability remains limited.
weaknesses: The central practical efficiency claim remains incompletely established. Cascading results measure accumulated parameter usage rather than actual adaptive inference latency. Appendix G.2 benchmarks fixed exits, excluding routing and shrinking-batch overhead, and finds TPCs slower at small batch sizes. End-to-end savings, including activation extraction, are not demonstrated.

The BeaverTails task construction needs clarification. Its safety annotations concern responses in prompt–response pairs, whereas the paper describes prompt-only inputs and harmful-prompt labels. The manuscript does not explain label conversion, treatment of conflicting labels across responses to the same prompt, or grouping repeated prompts when splitting data. These details materially affect the validity of the second benchmark.

The evidence supports improved benchmark classification more directly than stronger safety guarantees. Aggregate F1 and global calibration do not establish harmful-input recall at a controlled false-positive rate or reliability among early-exiting examples. WildGuardMix includes adversarial prompts, but there is no evaluation against attacks targeting the monitor or a dedicated distribution-shift assessment.

The novelty is primarily a combination of existing symmetric polynomial models, stagewise training, and confidence-based early exits. Comparisons with a progressively trained additive MLP or a simple linear-to-MLP cascade would help establish whether polynomial structure is essential to the gains. The training comparison also gives each polynomial term 50 epochs while joint baselines receive 50 epochs total.

Increasing degree does not consistently improve held-out performance; several appendix curves plateau or regress. Cascade experiments use only one seed, and the highlighted category-level gains lack sample counts and uncertainty estimates. Consequently, the strongest safety-dial and subgroup-improvement claims exceed the demonstrated reliability.

The interpretability demonstration is limited to quadratic contributions for one example, without semantic interpretation, intervention validation, or explanations of the full fifth-order model. It demonstrates faithful logit decomposition rather than broadly useful understanding of safety decisions.

strengths: TPCs offer a clear, practical extension of linear probes: progressive training preserves the original linear classifier and produces nested nonlinear classifiers supporting both fixed-budget inference and confidence-based early exits.

The evaluation is substantial: four LLMs, two datasets, multiple layers, five training seeds for the main comparisons, independently tuned parameter-matched MLPs, and an early-exit MLP baseline. Results generally support competitive predictive performance.
The appendix provides useful ablations on progressive training, polynomial degree, factorization rank, and symmetric parameterization, alongside calibration plots and latency measurements.

The polynomial formulation permits exact algebraic attribution of pairwise contributions to classifier logits. The paper appropriately acknowledges that these contributions are not necessarily human-interpretable.
weaknesses: The central computational benefit is not fully demonstrated in deployment terms. Cascade experiments measure summed active parameter counts, while the latency benchmarks evaluate fixed exits rather than actual adaptive execution. They therefore omit routing and variable-batch overhead. Figure 12 also shows higher TPC latency in several settings, especially small batches. End-to-end measurements including activation extraction would clarify the practical significance of saving compute on already tiny probes.

The BeaverTails task construction needs clarification. Its safety annotations concern prompt–response pairs, whereas the paper describes using prompt-only activations and harmful-prompt labels. It does not explain how response labels become prompt labels, how conflicting labels for repeated prompts are handled, or whether splitting prevents identical prompts from appearing across partitions. This leaves the validity and independence of this benchmark unresolved.

The stronger-guardrails framing exceeds the evidence. Higher polynomial degrees do not consistently improve test F1, with several nonmonotonic curves in Figure 6. Aggregate F1 and ECE do not establish reliable harmful-request recall at a controlled false-positive rate or safe confidence-based exits under distribution shift. Although WildGuardMix includes adversarial prompts, there is no monitor-adaptive attack evaluation or cross-dataset transfer test.

The contribution combines established polynomial networks, greedy additive training, and confidence-based early exits. A progressively trained additive MLP or residual-probe cascade would help isolate the value of increasing polynomial degree from the value of retaining a strong linear predictor and adding corrections. The joint-training ablation also gives each progressive term 50 epochs versus 50 epochs total for the joint model, confounding training strategy with optimization budget.

The most important adaptive results use only one seed, according to Appendix F.1, despite five-seed fixed-order comparisons. Category-specific improvements are highlighted without category sample counts or uncertainty estimates, and several overall gains over nonlinear baselines are modest. A validation-selected cascade operating point with repeated-seed test results would strengthen the evidence.

The interpretability demonstration is limited to one prompt and second-order interactions, without validating semantic meaning or explaining the complete higher-order prediction. Reproducibility is also incomplete: the supplied manuscript has a blank code link, and details such as feature scaling and threshold selection remain underspecified.

strengths: The method is clearly formulated and straightforward to implement. Progressive training preserves the original linear probe exactly while providing reusable higher-order classifiers and confidence-based early exits.

The experimental coverage is substantial: four backbone models, two training datasets, multiple layers, five training seeds for the main comparisons, parameter-matched nonlinear baselines, and extensive rank, degree, and training ablations.

TPCs outperform both MLP variants on WildGuardMix across all four backbones in Table 1. Cross-dataset results are also encouraging: on ToxicChat, TPC achieves 57.66 F1 versus 52.97 for EE-MLP and 46.27 for the linear probe.

The cascade experiments demonstrate useful reductions in evaluated parameters while retaining full-model performance. The appendix additionally includes calibration analysis, computational complexity, and latency measurements.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental: symmetric low-rank polynomial networks, greedy stagewise optimization, and confidence-based cascades are established components. Comparisons against a progressively trained additive MLP or residual ensemble would help establish whether polynomial structure contributes beyond the training and cascading strategy.

The central efficiency claim is not fully demonstrated in deployment terms. Cascade savings are measured through accumulated parameter counts, whereas the latency experiments benchmark fixed-depth evaluation rather than actual adaptive execution. Routing, shrinking batches, activation extraction, and end-to-end monitoring overhead remain unmeasured; TPCs are also slower than EE-MLPs at small batch sizes.

Aggregate accuracy advantages over strong nonlinear baselines are often small. WildGuardMix improvements over the standalone MLP range from 0.09 to 0.71 F1 points, and TPC loses to EE-MLP on three of four BeaverTails settings. Five-seed averages are useful, but paired test-set uncertainty is needed to establish the reliability of these differences; the cascade experiments use only one seed.

The progressive-training ablation compares against optimizing only the final polynomial output, which does not directly encourage useful intermediate predictions. Joint supervision of every truncation is a more informative alternative. Training budgets also differ: TPC receives 50 epochs per term, while jointly trained baselines receive 50 epochs total.

The safety-dial interpretation is stronger than the evidence. Additional terms do not consistently improve test performance, and aggregate F1 and ECE do not establish harmful-request recall at a controlled false-positive rate or the reliability of confident early exits under distribution shift. Cross-dataset evaluation covers only one backbone/layer and does not validate adaptive cascading.

Interpretability is demonstrated only through an algebraic decomposition of one quadratic prediction. The displayed neuron interactions lack semantic interpretation and contribute little individually to the total logit; there is no evidence that these explanations support practical auditing or remain useful at higher degrees.

strengths: The method is clear and technically plausible: progressively trained polynomial terms preserve the original linear probe while providing nested classifiers and confidence-based early exits.

The experimental coverage is substantial: four main backbones, two training datasets, five random seeds for the main comparisons, separately tuned parameter-matched baselines, and extensive rank, layer, degree, and training ablations.

There is concrete positive evidence. TPCs outperform the MLP baselines on WildGuardMix across the four models in Table 1. Cross-dataset results are also promising: ToxicChat F1 increases from 46.27 for linear probes and 52.97 for EE-MLPs to 57.66 for TPCs.

The polynomial representation supports exact algebraic attribution of interaction contributions. The appendix provides useful implementation details, complexity analysis, calibration results, and latency benchmarks.
weaknesses: The central practical benefit of adaptive computation remains incompletely demonstrated. Cascade experiments measure accumulated parameter usage, while Appendix G.2 benchmarks fixed-depth execution rather than actual conditional routing. Thus, batching, routing overhead, and end-to-end monitoring savings are unmeasured. This matters because probe costs are already tiny relative to the backbone, and TPCs are slower than EE-MLPs at small batch sizes.

The comparisons do not isolate the advantage of progressively increasing polynomial degree. A linear-probe-to-MLP cascade and a progressively trained additive neural classifier would be particularly informative. The training ablation compares against optimizing only the final polynomial output, which is not designed to preserve intermediate predictions; jointly supervising every polynomial prefix would provide a stronger alternative.

Static improvements over nonlinear baselines are often small or inconsistent. In Table 1, WildGuardMix gains over MLPs range from 0.09 to 0.71 F1 points, the bilinear probe exceeds TPC on Llama, and EE-MLPs outperform TPCs on three of four BeaverTails backbones. These results support competitiveness more clearly than a substantial predictive advance.

The 'stronger safety with more compute' framing exceeds the evidence. Performance is not monotonic with polynomial degree, as the authors acknowledge. Aggregate F1 and calibration plots do not establish harmful-request recall at controlled false-positive rates or reliability among confidently exited examples. Existing adversarial prompts and cross-dataset tests are useful, but do not establish robustness against attacks targeting the monitor.

The interpretability evidence is limited to a quadratic decomposition for one example. Exact contributions from unnamed residual-stream coordinates do not establish human-understandable explanations or causal safety mechanisms, and the example does not explain the complete degree-five classifier. The authors appropriately acknowledge the lack of semantic legibility.

Novelty is primarily the combination of established polynomial parameterizations, stagewise fitting, and confidence-based cascades. This is a potentially useful contribution, but stronger comparative evidence and measured adaptive-execution benefits are needed to make it clearly competitive for acceptance.

strengths: The method is clearly formulated and technically plausible. Progressive training preserves the linear probe exactly while producing useful nested polynomial classifiers, supporting both fixed-budget evaluation and confidence-based early exits.

The evaluation is substantial: four principal backbone models, two training datasets, parameter-matched MLP and early-exit baselines, five training seeds for the main comparisons, and extensive rank, degree, layer, and training ablations.

TPCs consistently outperform the MLP variants on WildGuardMix in Table 1. Cross-dataset results are also encouraging: on ToxicChat, TPC achieves 57.66 F1 versus 52.97 for the early-exit MLP and 46.27 for the linear probe.

The polynomial representation permits exact algebraic attribution of interaction contributions. The manuscript appropriately acknowledges that these dense neuron-level explanations are not necessarily human-interpretable.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the approach combines established symmetric polynomial parameterizations, stagewise additive training, and confidence-based cascading. Comparisons with progressively trained additive MLPs or residual probe ensembles would better isolate whether polynomial interactions provide an advantage beyond the training and cascade structure. Training budgets also differ: each polynomial term receives 50 epochs, whereas jointly trained baselines receive 50 epochs total.

The central computational-savings claim is not fully demonstrated in deployment terms. Cascade experiments primarily measure accumulated parameter usage; Appendix G.2 benchmarks fixed exits rather than actual adaptive execution. Routing overhead, batch fragmentation, activation extraction, and end-to-end latency remain unmeasured. The very small probe overhead relative to backbone computation also leaves the practical significance of these savings uncertain.

Aggregate gains over strong nonlinear baselines are generally modest. In Table 1, WildGuardMix improvements over standalone MLPs range from 0.09 to 0.71 F1 points, while TPC trails early-exit MLPs on three of four BeaverTails comparisons. Five-seed averages are useful, but paired test-set uncertainty is needed to establish the reliability of small differences; cascade experiments use only one seed.

The framing of additional compute as buying stronger guardrails exceeds the evidence. Performance is not monotonic with degree, as the paper acknowledges. F1 and aggregate calibration do not establish improved harmful-request recall at a fixed false-positive rate, nor do they characterize confidently incorrect early exits. Validation-selected cascade operating points and safety-relevant risk–cost curves would strengthen the central claim.

The interpretability demonstration is narrow: one quadratic example with individual contributions around 0.005 against a total logit of 18.11. It establishes an exact decomposition, but does not show that the highlighted interactions explain a substantial share of the decision or help diagnose monitoring failures, particularly for higher-degree models.
